691.event_title: Voltaire at the court of Frederick the Great
691.place: Berlin and Potsdam, Prussia (now Germany); Frankfurt
691.event: After years of admiring correspondence, Voltaire accepted Frederick II's pressing invitation and set out for Berlin on 28 June 1750, at first enchanted by life at the Prussian court in Berlin and Potsdam. Difficulties soon arose, and when he ridiculed Maupertuis, president of Frederick's Berlin Academy, in the pamphlet Diatribe du docteur Akakia (1752), the enraged king had it burned and gave its author a thorough dressing down. Voltaire left Prussia on 26 March 1753 and, on the journey home, was held under house arrest at an inn in Frankfurt by order of the Prussian resident.
691.explanation: The greatest writer of the age moved from flattering distance into the king's daily circle, and the very closeness that warmed him exposed him to the royal temper.
691.tie_back: Voltaire found that a powerful and changeable king is like a fire: welcome at a respectful distance, but scorching to one who settles too close and takes liberties beside it.
691._accuracy_note: A close illustration of the warmth and danger of nearness to a volatile monarch, though the quarrel began with a dispute between courtiers rather than with Frederick himself.

692.event_title: Belisarius refuses the crown the Goths offered him at Ravenna
692.event: By 540 the hard-pressed Ostrogoths in Italy offered to surrender to the Byzantine general Belisarius if he would rule over them as emperor. Belisarius, who served the emperor Justinian, dissembled: he accepted the Goths' capitulation at Ravenna and then refused the title, claiming the kingdom and its treasury in Justinian's name. Justinian, who had already come to fear that so popular a commander might aim at his throne, recalled him from Italy.
692.explanation: The one prize a ruler most jealously guards is his own crown, and Belisarius pointedly declined to reach for it even when it was offered to him.
692.tie_back: The kural advises the servant not to covet what the king himself desires, and Belisarius turned down the very throne that Justinian held dear.
692._accuracy_note: A strong example of refusing to covet the ruler's prize, but it also shows the limits of the kural's promise, since Justinian's suspicion was not fully relieved.

693.event_title: Naser al-Din Shah turns against his reforming minister Amir Kabir
693.event: Mirza Taqi Khan, known as Amir Kabir, helped secure the throne for the young Naser al-Din Shah in 1848 and as chief minister launched sweeping reforms, including the founding of the Dar al-Fonun college. His reforms antagonized excluded notables, who formed a coalition against him in which the queen mother was active, and she convinced the young shah that the minister wanted to usurp the throne. In the autumn of 1851 the shah dismissed him and exiled him to Kashan, where he was put to death on the shah's orders in January 1852.
693.explanation: The minister's record of service and even his marriage to the shah's sister could not undo the suspicion once it had been planted in the ruler's mind.
693.tie_back: The kural warns that once a king has grown suspicious, no one can set his mind at rest, and no past loyalty saved Amir Kabir once the shah came to believe he sought the throne.
693._accuracy_note: A clear case of royal suspicion proving impossible to dispel, though the suspicion was sown by rivals rather than by any grave fault of Amir Kabir's own.

694.event_title: Lord Chesterfield warns his son against audible laughter in polite company
694.event: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield, a British statesman and diplomat who served as secretary of state from 1746 to 1748, wrote a long series of letters of advice on manners and worldly success to his son Philip. In a letter dated Bath, 9 March 1748, he warned his son that he hoped he would often be seen to smile but never heard to laugh, calling audible laughter ill-bred and a mark of folly. The letters, not written for publication, later appeared as Letters to His Son and became famous as guides to the art of pleasing.
694.explanation: A seasoned courtier passed on the rule that in polished society the face may show pleasure but must not break into the private, noisy mirth that offends others.
694.tie_back: Like the kural, which tells the courtier to suppress shared smiles and whispers before the great, Chesterfield counselled restraint of laughter in the company one must please.
694._accuracy_note: Chesterfield addresses laughter in good company generally rather than whispering or shared glances before a ruler, so the fit is reasonable but partial.

695.event_title: Senator Truman stops probing the secret Manhattan Project
695.event: As chairman of a Senate committee reviewing defense spending, Harry Truman noticed large sums flowing into an unexplained wartime project and asked Secretary of War Henry Stimson about it. Stimson told him the matter was secret for reasons of national security, and Truman dropped the inquiry. He learned the details of the atomic bomb project only after becoming president on 12 April 1945, receiving a full briefing from Stimson on 25 April.
695.explanation: A vigorous investigator accepted that some state secrets were not his to pry into, and waited until the secret was properly entrusted to him.
695.tie_back: The kural tells the servant not to eavesdrop or press with questions when the ruler deals in secrets, but to hear them only when they are freely told, which is exactly how Truman came to know of the bomb.
695._accuracy_note: A close match for restraint toward secret counsel, though Truman deferred to a cabinet secretary's request rather than to a king.

696.event_title: Galileo names Jupiter's moons the Medicean Stars
696.event: In January 1610 Galileo discovered four moons orbiting Jupiter and published the findings in Sidereus Nuncius in March 1610. He had written to his former pupil, Grand Duke Cosimo II de' Medici, about the discoveries and named the moons the Medicean Stars, announcing the name on the book's title page and in a dedication, and he sent the Grand Duke a copy together with the telescope he had used. The Grand Duke was pleased and invited Galileo to become Philosopher and Mathematician to the court in Florence, which Galileo accepted.
696.explanation: Galileo presented a discovery that challenged the prevailing view of the heavens in a form his prince was glad to receive, and so won the patronage to keep working.
696.tie_back: The kural asks the counsellor to read the ruler, choose the moment and say what is needful in a way he will want to hear, as Galileo did by offering an important truth wrapped in an honour to the Medici.
696._accuracy_note: A strong example of timing and pleasing presentation before a ruler, though Galileo was seeking a post rather than serving as an established court adviser.

697.event_title: Bismarck persuades King Wilhelm I to make a lenient peace at Nikolsburg
697.event: After Prussia's victory over Austria at Koniggratz in July 1866, King Wilhelm I wanted to take territory from Austria and from Saxony, which he regarded as a legitimate war trophy, and senior officers pressed to cross the Danube. Bismarck, who had no interest in taking land from Austria and did not want to make it a lasting enemy, opposed these demands; he later claimed he came close to resigning and was saved when the Crown Prince persuaded his father to accept Bismarck's terms. The preliminary peace signed at Nikolsburg on 26 July 1866 took no Austrian territory for Prussia and left Saxony intact.
697.explanation: Bismarck refused to serve up the trophies his king wanted, and the moderate peace kept the door open to later friendship with Austria.
697.tie_back: The kural says a counsellor should speak only of what truly benefits the king and never of what is useless or harmful, even when the king himself asks for it, and Bismarck held to that line against his own sovereign.
697._accuracy_note: A close illustration of advising against a ruler's harmful wish, though Bismarck's own account of the crisis may dramatize his role.

698.event_title: Peter the Great removes his half-sister Sophia from power
698.event: Sophia Alekseyevna ruled Russia as regent from 1682 for her brother Ivan V and her younger half-brother Peter, who were proclaimed joint tsars, and she used grand royal titles while the boy Peter lived away from the Kremlin. In July 1689 the seventeen-year-old Peter clashed with her publicly in Moscow's Kazan Cathedral, and when Sophia tried to turn the streltsy against his family, many of their colonels supported Peter instead. In September 1689 Peter overthrew her, she was denied her royal titles, and she was confined in the Novodevichy Convent in Moscow.
698.explanation: Sophia had treated the crowned tsar as a junior relative to be managed, and the young ruler's authority asserted itself the moment he came of age.
698.tie_back: The kural warns against slighting a ruler because he is younger or a relative, and Sophia lost everything by treating the tsar as merely her younger half-brother.
698._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit, since Sophia was an ambitious regent rather than a courtier, but she did fail to respect the dignity of a younger kinsman who held the crown.

699.event_title: The Earl of Essex deserts his post in Ireland and loses Elizabeth's favour
699.place: Ireland and London, England, United Kingdom
699.event: Robert Devereux, 2nd Earl of Essex, was Queen Elizabeth I's favourite, and for years she put up with his rashness, even after he turned his back on her during a dispute. Sent to Ireland as lord lieutenant in 1599, he concluded an unfavourable truce and, defying the queen's instructions, suddenly returned to England to justify himself to her privately. She placed him under house arrest and deprived him of his offices in June 1600, and after a failed attempt to raise London in revolt in February 1601 he was tried and executed for treason.
699.explanation: Essex mistook years of indulgence for licence and did what the queen had forbidden, trusting her affection to cover it.
699.tie_back: The kural says people of steady judgement never think the king favours them and so do what the king would not accept, the very error that ruined Essex.
699._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of presuming on royal favour, though Essex's later rebellion went far beyond the kind of misstep the kural describes.

700.event_title: The fall of Ibrahim Pasha, Suleyman the Magnificent's boyhood companion
700.event: Ibrahim, a slave of Christian birth from near Parga, became the inseparable companion of the future Sultan Suleyman before his accession, and in 1523 Suleyman raised him over more senior officials to be grand vizier, later marrying a sister to him. For thirteen years he ran the empire's affairs and led campaigns in Hungary and Persia, but he was unpopular with the Ottoman elite for his reputation for arrogance and was reported to have boasted publicly of his power over the sultan's decisions. Alarmed by his usurpation of the titles of sovereignty, Suleyman had him put to death in March 1536.
700.explanation: The closeness of a lifelong friendship gave Ibrahim power, but it also led him to behave as an equal of the sultan, and that familiarity ended in his ruin.
700.tie_back: The kural warns that the familiarity which makes a man act improperly because he is an old friend of the king will bring him to ruin, and Ibrahim's story fits it closely.
700._accuracy_note: A very close fit, though historians debate the exact causes of his fall and court intrigue also played a part.
